obtained.how: open-access PDF from the publisher (PLOS ONE printable version)

bibliography.checked_against: Crossref and the title page (PLoS ONE 13(3): e0194092, published 15 March 2018; nine authors as listed)

claims.claim: across seven piscivores (bass, pike and five others) the median prey is 10–20 % and the largest 32–46 % of the predator's length
claims.source_value: abstract: 'generally ranged from 10–20% and 32–46%'; these are the interquartile ranges of the model estimates (relative IP50 = 50th-percentile regression; relative IPmax = 99th-percentile regression, 95th for rock bass) across taxa over the 5th–95th percentiles of predator length; the full ranges are 9–25 % and 32–57 %
claims.quote: generally ranged from 10–20% and 32–46% of predator total length, respectively
claims.conditions: field diets (lavage, tube, dissection) from lakes and reservoirs in Alberta, Illinois, Minnesota, New York and Wisconsin, 1976–2013; prey and predator total length; seven taxa (crappie grouped), with largemouth, smallmouth, rock bass, muskellunge, pike, walleye
claims.note: the digits are the abstract's, but the abstract says 'generally', and p. 6 shows both are interquartile ranges ('interquartile range ... spanning from 32–46%'; relative IPmax 'ranged from 32–57%', relative IP50 '9–25%'). A light fix: 'generally (interquartile range) 10–20 % and 32–46 %, at most 25 % and 57 %'. Seven taxa is right (crappie grouped)

claims.claim: field maxima across piscivores are 0.32–0.46 of the predator's length
claims.source_value: relative IPmax (99th-percentile regression) 32–57 % across taxa and predator lengths; 32–46 % is its interquartile range; for fusiform prey 33–49 % (IQR), laterally compressed 4–39 %
claims.quote: for the 5th to 95th percentile range of predator total lengths ranged from 32–57%
claims.conditions: 99th-percentile quantile regressions; 5th–95th percentile of each predator's length
claims.note: as 'the field's maxima' the range is 32–57 % (IQR 32–46 %); relative IPmax was fairly constant with length for muskellunge and pike and fell with length for walleye, largemouth and smallmouth (p. 6)

claims.claim: the data include 784 pike and 201 smallmouth bass diets
claims.conditions: 'Predator sample size' (fish with fish in the diet); prey items 2,233 (pike) and 380 (smallmouth); pike from Alberta and Minnesota, smallmouth from Minnesota, New York and Wisconsin
claims.note: read in the raw text (the layout text shifts this table's rows: it puts 201 beside rock bass)

claims.claim: on their smallmouth regressions, bass of 200, 300 and 400 mm take median prey of about 50, 54 and 62 mm (project calculation)
claims.location: p. 5, Table 2 (smallmouth: Prey TL = exp(α + β·predator TL²)); p. 8, Table 3 (50th: α 3.83, β 1.82e-06)
claims.conditions: 50th-percentile quantile regression, all prey shapes; smallmouth predators ~200–460 mm (5th–95th percentile, Fig. 1 top axis), so 200–400 mm is inside the modelled range

claims.claim: the smallest prey of field piscivores barely rise with their size
claims.quote: this accounted for an increase of only 7–14 mm for all taxa
claims.conditions: IPmin (1st-percentile regression) from the 5th to the 95th percentile of predator length; muskellunge the exception (+26 mm)

notes: Useful beyond the citing sentences: the median prey of pike, walleye and smallmouth rose only 40–53 % across their length range, while muskellunge and largemouth rose >200 % (p. 6); modal prey lengths fell within 16–73 mm for every taxon and length except large muskellunge (p. 6); median log10 predator:prey mass ratios 1.9–2.5. Pike data are from Alberta (Diana) and Minnesota; no chain pickerel. The corrections are one reading in two places: the 10–20 % and 32–46 % are interquartile ranges ('generally'), not the full ranges (9–25 % and 32–57 %); every number checks.
